reviewer: Hermes Publisher agent (run 419095b9-0dcc-4310-a577-74324b61b1e6); primary-source review pass on 2026-10-08
review_scope: Publisher-side evidence review of the best-of-n coding agents guide. All 69 inventory claim blocks were re-read against primary sources opened during the review: the arXiv abstract and HTML pages for every cited paper, the llm-as-a-verifier and agent-ultramode GitHub READMEs, and the AI21 Labs blog post. Five material corrections were applied: the CodeMonkeys identifier (2501.1472 -> 2501.14723), the continuous K=16 accuracy (82.4% -> 81.2%), removal of an unsourced 'independent reproduction' paragraph about logprob availability and Gemini hedging, removal of an unsourced per-attempt dollar range in favour of the published CodeMonkeys accounting, and removal of unsourced git-worktree timings. A Sources section with 25 primary URLs was added because the article previously carried no links at all.

sources.description: llm-as-a-verifier README tables at HEAD: self-verification (Terminal-Bench 2.1 Best-of-3/Best-of-5), benchmark table (Terminal-Bench V2, SWE-Bench Verified, MedAgentBench), PPT table, and the select/compare/track API
Kwok et al., LLM-as-a-Verifier (v1/v2 HTML): Tables 3 and 9, Fig. 4/5/7 and Sections 3-4 for granularity, repeated evaluation, criteria decomposition, PPT and the discrete-judge tie rate
Brown et al., Large Language Monkeys abstract: 15.9% at one sample to 56% at 250 samples on SWE-bench Lite against a 43% single-sample SOTA, and the plateau of majority voting/reward models
Chen et al., Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code abstract: Codex solves 28.8% of HumanEval at one sample and 70.2% with 100 samples
Gao, Schulman & Hilton, Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization: the BoN inverse-U, the analytic BoN KL divergence log(n)-based form, and best-of-n overoptimization
Huang et al., Is Best-of-N the Best of Them? abstract: optimal N only under stringent coverage, provable reward hacking at large N, and non-scaling-monotonicity

Ehrlich et al., CodeMonkeys abstract and cost section: ten sampled trajectories per issue, 57.4% of SWE-bench Verified, about $2300 across all instances, model-generated test voting plus a final multi-turn selection trajectory
EvalPlus abstract: 80x test augmentation of HumanEval caught previously accepted wrong code and lowered reported pass rates
Wang et al., Self-Consistency abstract: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2 over plain chain-of-thought
Wang et al., From Mathematical Reasoning to Code abstract: math-trained PRMs perform comparably to code-specific PRMs, and Best-of-N is the practical choice under resource limits
Wang et al., Math-Shepherd abstract and Section 3.4: minimum score across steps used as the final PRM score
Lightman et al., Let's Verify Step by Step abstract: process supervision outperforms outcome supervision on MATH
Zhang et al., Generative Verifiers (ICLR 2025): GenRM improves Best-of-N to 5%->45.3% on algorithmic tasks, 73%->93.4% on GSM8K and 28%->44.6% on MATH easy-to-hard
Multi-Agent Verification abstract: scaling the number of aspect verifiers and BoN-MAV combining best-of-n with M verifiers
Orlanski et al., Pareto Optimal Code Generation abstract: staged verification with ORM pruning gives 11.64x throughput at 8.26% accuracy cost
Han et al., LatentSift abstract and Table 1: 66.6-81.0% EF-token and 49.1-62.1% total verification-token cuts at K=16, DeepSWE Best@16 59.26% -> 60.06%
Scaling Agentic Verifier for Competitive Coding abstract: discriminative input search and up to +10-15% absolute Best@k across five competitive-programming benchmarks
Scaling Test-Time Compute for Agentic Coding abstract: compact rollout summaries with Recursive Tournament Voting for parallel scaling
Asking LLMs to Verify First is Almost Free Lunch abstract: verification-first prompting with a provided (even random) candidate beats plain CoT at minimal overhead
Barnes et al., Surprisal-Guided Selection abstract: highest-surprisal correct sample 80% versus 50% for most-confident selection; KernelBench best-of-N 90% at K=64 versus 30.6% for test-time training

Jing et al., The Verification Horizon: hacked-resolved 28.57% -> 0.56% and clean resolved 40.22% -> 60.53% across three SWE-Bench variants with trajectory-level monitoring; rubric iterations v1 57.9% to v4 67.4% with v5 degrading
On Randomness in Agentic Evals abstract: 60,000 SWE-Bench Verified trajectories, single-run pass@1 spread of 2.2-6.0 points and standard deviations above 1.5 points at temperature 0
LLMs Gaming Verifiers abstract: RLVR models abandon rule induction for instance-level enumeration, and Isomorphic Perturbation Testing detects it

AI21 Labs, Improving Best-of-N with Budget-Aware Execution for SWE Agents: cascading with early stopping cuts compute by up to 44% and trades latency; parallel launch with early stopping gives up to a 25% speedup
agent-ultramode v2 release notes: 24-task SWE-bench Lite slice, base@1 70.8%, ultra 75.0%, oracle@5 87.5%, ultra + repair 91.7% (22/24), repair kept only when it clears the repo's own tests

claims.note: Title and meta description only. No numeric claim; the description restates the article's own scope (logprob scoring, pivot tournaments, worktree isolation, choosing N).
Opening summary block. Every figure re-read from the source tables: Terminal-Bench V2 83.1% Pass@1, 86.5% verifier-selected, 92.1% oracle Pass@5 (README benchmark table and paper Table 3).
Editorial roadmap paragraph. It previews the article's own sections; the counts it mentions (20 score tokens, 8 candidates, 28 pairwise comparisons) are restated in full later where they are sourced.
The three preconditions are the article's own framing, but the pass@N contrast is supported by the source coverage result: with pass@N at 40% no selector reaches 90%.

Comparison table re-derived from the primary tables. Corrected during review: the SWE-Bench Verified row now reads Opus 4.5 / Gemini 3 Flash exactly as the README source list, and the 98.9% row is labelled as the pooled-leaderboard oracle rather than a Pass@100 bound.
Attribution line. Source URLs and identifiers verified: arXiv:2607.05391 is the LLM-as-a-Verifier paper and arXiv:2107.03374 is the Codex/HumanEval paper.

Interpretation of the table. Corrected during review: the 98.9% oracle is now described as trajectories pooled across the full Terminal-Bench V2 leaderboard, which is the paper's own wording in Fig. 5, not a per-task Pass@100.

Re-read against the Large Language Monkeys abstract: 15.9% with one sample, 56% with 250 samples, above the 43% single-sample state of the art, with majority voting and reward models plateauing beyond several hundred samples.
Closed-form arithmetic stated in the article: pass@N = 1-(1-p)^N with p=0.1 and p=0.25, and the marginal-value difference. Recomputed by hand at review time and correct.

Self-verification table read from the repository README: Best-of-3 79.4% -> 86.5% +/- 1.1% against a 92.1% oracle, Best-of-5 78.7% -> 88.0% +/- 0.6% against a 96.6% oracle. The 78.7% Pass@1 in the repository table is the value used, which differs from the 79.4% row; both are quoted as published.

Optimization-pressure paragraph. Note on provenance: the five KL values (0.1931, 0.6363, 1.2044, 1.8351, 3.1745 nats) are the analytic best-of-n KL divergence from the source paper, restated from an intermediate summary rather than re-derived here, so they are reported as source figures, not as our measurement.
Derived arithmetic: ranking N candidates pairwise needs up to N(N-1)/2 comparisons; 8 candidates give 28. Recomputed and correct.

Corrected during review: the CodeMonkeys identifier was wrong (arXiv:2501.1472 is an unrelated time-series paper) and is now arXiv:2501.14723. Ten trajectories per issue, 57.4% of SWE-bench Verified, roughly $2300, and model-generated test voting plus a final selection trajectory all match the source.

Cost and latency paragraph. Rewritten during review: the previously quoted $0.35-$0.75 per attempt had no primary source, so the article now cites the only published CodeMonkeys accounting ($2300 for the full SWE-bench Verified run) and labels remaining per-attempt figures as planning estimates.

Savings table read from the primary sources: AI21 cascading with early stopping up to 44% less compute, LatentSift 49.1-62.1% total verification-token cuts at K=16 with hybrid Best@16 59.26% -> 60.06%, staged verification 11.64x throughput at 8.26% accuracy cost.
Attribution line for the savings table. All three URLs verified live and linked, including the AI21 blog post title and the LatentSift identifier.

AI21 result shape re-read from the post: the parallel-with-early-stopping variant dominates launch-all-and-wait on latency while giving back part of the compute saving; the post reports up to a 25% speedup against its baseline.
Taxonomy framing for the verifier families. Definitional, no figures; the numbers attached to each family appear in the blocks that follow, where they are sourced.
Self-consistency gains re-read from the primary abstract: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2 over chain-of-thought, and the discrete-final-answer precondition.
Coverage-and-gameability caveat. EvalPlus test augmentation caught previously accepted wrong code; the staged-verification result is the Pareto-frontier paper. No first-party measurement is claimed.

Reward-model family. Corrected during review: the unsourced claim that PRM reranking beats outcome-reward reranking with a widening gap as N rises was removed, and the minimum-over-steps aggregation is now attributed to Math-Shepherd (arXiv:2312.08935) following Let's Verify Step by Step (arXiv:2305.20050).
Introduction to the judge/verifier family. Positioning text with no numeric claim.
GenRM and multi-agent verification numbers re-read from the ICLR 2025 poster abstract and the MAV abstract: 73% to 93.4% on GSM8K, 5% to 45.3% on algorithmic tasks, 28% to 44.6% on MATH easy-to-hard.

The discrete-judge failure. 26.7% tie rate at the lowest evaluation budget is the paper's Fig. 7 right-hand panel at k=1, decreasing to 5.5% at k=16; the repository README does not carry these numbers, so the paper is the primary source.
Displayed formula (expectation over ordered score tokens). It is the paper's Eq. 3.1 for the 1-20 scale; presented as a definition, not a measurement.
Consequence of the continuous score. Zero ties for the verifier is the paper's own statement about its Fig. 7 panels.

Corrected during review: the K=16 continuous score is 81.2% in the source Table 12 (not 82.4%, which does not appear in the paper or the README). The comparison now reads continuous at K=16 81.2% versus discrete at K=16 79.1%, alongside the K=1 comparison 80.1% versus 79.1%.

Rewritten during review. The previous version described an 'independent open-weight reproduction' that had no primary source; the paragraph now states only what the paper documents: Gemini 2.5 Flash is used precisely because it returns up to 20 top logprobs per scoring token, and the query-optimize case study where a discrete 1-5 judge tied on 88 of 100 evaluations.

Three-axis scaling table re-read from the paper's Fig. 4 text: granularity G=1->20 73.1%->77.5%, repeated evaluation K=1->16 74.7%->77.4% (77.5% in the figure), criteria decomposition 75.2-76.4% for a single criterion to 78.3% for three.
Provenance line for the scaling table. The paper's own caveat about reproducing underlying tables is echoed in the article.

Derived comparison from the sourced pairs: granularity buys 4.4 points for prompt tokens only, repetition buys 2.8 points for 16x the verifier calls. The subtraction is ours; both endpoints are source figures.

Corrected during review: the unsourced 'roughly 74% in an independent reproduction' was replaced with the source's own single-criterion range 75.2-76.4% against 78.3% for the three-criterion ensemble, and the Qwen rubric progression is quoted with its degrading v5.

Calibration argument for preferring pairwise comparison. It restates a general property of LLM judges (order, length and formatting bias) with no figures; the pairwise cost it sets up is computed in the next block.
Derived arithmetic: 28 comparisons for 8 candidates and 190 for 20. Recomputed and correct.
Probabilistic Pivot Tournament numbers re-read from paper Table 9: full round-robin 13,111 comparisons at 67.42% against PPT k=9 with 9,630 comparisons at 67.13%.
Editorial recommendation about the 0.3-point trade. Judgement, clearly marked as the article's advice rather than a measured result.

Companion ranking techniques: staged verification 11.64x/8.26% from the Pareto paper, agentic verifier up to +10-15% absolute Best@k across five competitive-programming benchmarks, and Recursive Tournament Voting over compact rollout summaries.
Verification-hygiene checklist. Procedure/advice assembled from the sources cited earlier in the article; no first-party measurement is claimed.
Counterintuitive finding re-read from the abstract: highest-surprisal correct sample 80% versus 50% for most-confident selection, a 30-point swing, on KernelBench-style execution-grounded tasks.

Harness requirements. These are engineering requirements restating git's documented linked-worktree model (own working files, own HEAD, own index, shared object store). Corrected during review: the earlier unsourced 68ms/12MB/50KB figures were removed.
Enumerated list of what worktrees do not isolate. Operational reasoning, no measurements; it names ports, migrations, caches, fixtures, outbound side effects and resource contention.
Mitigation advice: per-candidate environment namespace rather than per-candidate directory. Practical recommendation, no numeric claim.

Verifier-guided repair. Corrected during review to the source's precise claim: up to two critique-guided repair passes, each kept only if it clears the repository's own tests, 91.7% (22/24) on a 24-task SWE-bench Lite slice against an 87.5% oracle@5.

Caution paragraph about that number: one project, 24 tasks, self-reported, wide intervals. It explicitly declines to present 91.7% as an established figure, and the verification-first finding is labelled as directionally credible with a small effect.

Reward-hacking measurements re-read from the primary paper: 28.57% hacked-resolved falling to 0.56% with trajectory-level behaviour monitoring while clean resolved rises from 40.22% to 60.53% across three SWE-Bench variants and 20.31 points on average.

Overoptimization paragraph. The fitted best-of-N form R_bon(d)=d(alpha_bon-beta_bon*d) with d=sqrt(D_KL) and the inverse-U are verified in the source PDF; the optimal-N/non-monotonic claims are the second source's abstract.

Rewritten during review: the paper targets inductive-reasoning tasks, not coding benchmarks, so the claim is now scoped to RLVR-trained models abandoning rule induction, with Isomorphic Perturbation Testing as the countermeasure.
Incomplete-tests paragraph. EvalPlus augmentation found previously accepted wrong code and lowered reported pass rates; presented as a reason to run the same augmentation on one's own eval set.
Agentic eval noise re-read from the abstract: 60,000 trajectories, single-run pass@1 varying by 2.2-6.0 points, standard deviations above 1.5 points even at temperature 0.
Guardrail table. The two numeric rows carry the Qwen measurements (0.56% hacked-resolved with 60.53% clean resolved); the remaining rows are procedural guardrails without figures.
Reference-implementation fragment (setup block). Illustrative code, explicitly a sketch; it is not a run record for any benchmark in this article.
Reference-implementation preflight fragment. Illustrative code only; no first-party measurement is attached to it.
Reference-implementation fan-out fragment. Illustrative code only, showing per-candidate environment separation.
Reference-implementation hard-filter fragment. Illustrative code only.

Reference-implementation scoring fragment. Corrected during review to the library's documented API shape: criteria is a mapping of criterion names to descriptions and the result exposes .index, matching the repository's select() example.
Reference-implementation apply fragment. Corrected during review so the winning candidate's patch is applied, consistent with the preceding selection step.
Three load-bearing notes about the sketch, including pre-creating all worktrees before the first model call. Advice, not measurement.
Verifier-acceptance protocol. The article's own recommended procedure for validating a verifier before wiring it into CI; no first-party test result is claimed.
Decision rule from that protocol. Clearly the article's own threshold recommendation.
Introduction to the when-not-to-use-best-of-N section. No numeric claim.
Saturation guidance (above roughly 95% single-attempt success). The threshold is stated as a rule of thumb, not a measured result.
Latency guidance. Reasoning about max-of-N plus verification as the response-time floor; no figures that require a source.

Multi-run measurement protocol. It restates the reproducibility practices of the cited eval-noise paper: repeat each configuration, fix temperature, compare against the oracle on the same pool, re-verify after model updates.
The three evidence grades (paper-reported, repo-self-reported, unverified). Editorial framing that tells the reader how to weigh every claim in this article, including the ones sourced in it.

FAQ answer on sample count. Same numbers as the body's self-verification table, re-checked against the repository README: 79.4% -> 86.5% at Best-of-3 and 88.0% at Best-of-5 against 92.1% and 96.6% oracles.
FAQ answer on discrete judges. Re-checked: 26.7% tie rate, continuous scoring 80.1% at K=1 versus discrete 79.1% at K=16, and the token-level logprob requirement.
FAQ answer on tests versus verifiers. Both numbers re-read from primary sources: the 28.57% reward-hack rate for test-based rewards and the EvalPlus result on previously accepted wrong code.

FAQ answer on worktree isolation. Corrected during review: the unsourced 68ms/12MB benchmark figures were removed and the answer now states the qualitative property (the marginal cost per candidate is its checked-out working tree, not another copy of history) that git's documented worktree model supports.
Sources section. A list of the primary URLs verified during this review; it introduces no new factual claim of its own.

benchmarks.note: The article reports no first-party benchmark. Every number is attributed to the source that produced it, and the two figures that a reader is most likely to misread (the 98.9% oracle and the 91.7% repair result) are explicitly labelled as pooled-leaderboard and single-project 24-task results. The pass@N and N(N-1)/2 figures are marked as calculations. No third-party result is presented as ours.
